doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Liner notes by Gitler, Morgenstern and Hentoff as his education in jazz writing
summary: Liner notes taught him more than the French histories of Hodeir and Panassie, which did not match Chicago jazz.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: It was an art and I think it really influenced my writing. That’s the nice thing. I mean liner notes were not — on rock records are very seldom any liner notes. If there were they were very jivey and hyped up. But on a jazz record, you’re reading Ira Gitler or Dan Morgenstern or Nat Hentoff, you’ve learned something about how the music was put together and who these people were. And it really helped me to figure out what jazz writing was about, more than the classic books that were available in the sixties, Hodier or Panassie. This did not strike me as being true of the jazz experience as I knew it, what they were writing.

Histories and they were really from the thirties, they were French, they had a completely different frame of contacts and it didn’t seem anything like what Chicago was in the fifties and sixties to me.
But Hentoff and Morgenstern and Gitler and a few other people touched on something that I could recognize.
